subtype: Approach: polishing the product before showing anyone [Pitfall]
passage:
Month one, Monday. Sonali changed the app's button colour for the fourth time and told her friend Maria, "I can't show it yet. First impressions matter."

Month three, Wednesday. The icons had been redrawn twice. Maria asked, "Has anyone outside your laptop seen this?" "Not yet." Sonali checked the bank balance and told herself it was still fine.

Month five, Friday. The app looked beautiful. The bank balance showed three months of cash left. Nobody had ever touched the app. Sonali sat with the number and felt the floor go a little soft. "I was scared of looking amateur," she said to Maria. "So I made sure nobody saw it at all."

qa.q: How much cash did Sonali have left in month five?
qa.a: She had three months of cash left.
Sonali was afraid of looking amateur.

qa.q: What could Sonali do now with three months left?
qa.a: Sonali could show a rough version to a few real users this week and let their feedback decide what to improve.

qa.q: How might Maria have seen Sonali's approach over the months?
qa.a: Maria was probably worried, as the question about whether anyone outside the laptop had seen it suggests.

grounding: Sonali keeps polishing the app for months from fear of a weak first impression while cash drains and no customer feedback arrives.

subtype: Approach: polishing the product before showing anyone [Pitfall]
passage:
Neelam ma'am closed her laptop when the young founder said he wanted two more months to polish before showing anyone. "Sit. Let me tell you about Divyansh. Years ago he came to me with savings for eight months and a lovely idea: an app for booking home cooks. He was twenty-four and terrified of looking amateur.
So he polished. New colours, new icons, smoother animations. Every time I asked, 'Has any customer used it?' he said, 'Not yet, it's not ready.' Five months went. His designer cost money. His rent cost money. When he finally showed it to real families, they said the booking steps were confusing and they wanted to pay in cash. Everything he had perfected was the wrong thing.
He had three months left by then. He didn't make it. He's fine now, a good product lead, but he tells everyone: show it rough, show it early."

qa.q: How many months of savings did Divyansh start with?
What was young Divyansh afraid of?
qa.a: He was terrified of looking amateur, which is why he kept polishing.

qa.q: Which choice in the story could have changed the ending?
qa.a: Showing the rough app to real families in the first month, so he would have learned early about the confusing booking steps and cash payments.

qa.q: How did the families who finally tried the app see it?
qa.a: They found the booking steps confusing and wanted to pay in cash, so the polish meant little to them.

grounding: It shows a young founder polishing an app for five months out of fear of a weak first impression, so money drains without feedback and only three months remain.

subtype: Approach: polishing the product before showing anyone [Pitfall]
passage:
Ojas had quit his job in February with savings for eight months and a plan for a fitness-class booking app. By March the logo had been redrawn four times. By April he was arguing with himself about button shadows at 2 am in his rented room in Indore, the fan off because the power kept cutting.
"Just show it to five gym owners," Gurpreet said on the phone. Gurpreet had been meant to handle sales but had taken a part-time job to pay rent and could only help on Sundays.
"Not yet. If the first impression is weak, they'll never look again."
In July, with the design finally perfect, Ojas showed it to a gym owner across town. The owner scrolled for a minute. "Nice. But my members book on the phone. Why would they use this?"
Ojas walked home and checked his bank balance. Three months left.

qa.q: How did the gym owner say members book?
Why did Ojas refuse to show it to five gym owners?
qa.a: Ojas was afraid that a weak first impression would make them never look again.

qa.q: What could Ojas have done in March instead of redrawing the logo?
qa.a: He could have shown a rough version to a few gym owners and learned early that members book by phone.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel about the July meeting?
qa.a: Gurpreet may feel frustrated and worried, having urged Ojas to show gym owners months earlier while the money ran down.

grounding: It shows a founder refining an app for five months for fear of a weak first impression, so savings drain without customer feedback and three months are left.
